You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces - posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 30
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      # Run the (no-cost, no-API) Vogon canary against each checkpoint backend so
      # the git-refs store is guarded on every PR alongside the default git-branch.
      matrix:
        checkpoint_store: [git-branch, git-refs]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
        with:
          ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha || github.sha }}
      - uses: jdx/mise-action@f10502fc09dadecfefb962fff68ce77213930204 # v4
      - name: E2E Canary
        env:
          E2E_CHECKPOINT_STORE: ${{ matrix.checkpoint_store }}
        run: mise run test:e2e:canary

  test-windows:
    runs-on: windows-latest
    timeout-minutes: 10
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
        with:
          ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha || github.sha }}
      - name: Windows PowerShell 5 installer syntax
        shell: powershell
        run: |
          if ($PSVersionTable.PSVersion.Major -ne 5) {
            throw "Expected Windows PowerShell 5.x, got $($PSVersionTable.PSVersion)"
          }
          .\scripts\install.ps1 -Help
      - name: PowerShell 7 installer syntax
        shell: pwsh
        run: |
          if ($PSVersionTable.PSVersion.Major -lt 7) {
            throw "Expected PowerShell 7 or later, got $($PSVersionTable.PSVersion)"
          }
          .\scripts\install.ps1 -Help
      - uses: actions/setup-go@b7ad1dad31e06c5925ef5d2fc7ad053ef454303e # v7.0.0
        with:
          go-version-file: go.mod
      # Real-Windows tests must include Windows or MSYS in their top-level
      # test name so this job selects them without running POSIX-only harnesses.
      - name: Windows unit tests
        run: go test ./cmd/entire/cli/... -run '(Windows|MSYS)' -count=1 -v

  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    needs:
      - test-core

# Install Provenance And Auto-Update Plan

## Goal

Add installer-owned install provenance for released binaries, then build auto-update on top of that provenance.

## Scope For The Next PR

1. Define the provenance file format.
   Example fields:
   - `manager`: `install.sh`, `brew`, `scoop`
   - `channel`: `stable`, `nightly`
   - `package`: `entire`, `entire@nightly`, `entire/cli`
   - `installed_at`: timestamp

2. Make each installer write the provenance file.
   - `install.sh` writes it directly.
   - Homebrew formula/cask writes it in package-managed install hooks.
   - Scoop manifest writes it in `post_install`.

3. Keep the CLI read-only for provenance.
   - The CLI reads `install.json`.
   - If the file is missing, it may infer update hints for backward compatibility.
   - The CLI must not create or overwrite provenance.

4. Add auto-update on top of installer-owned provenance.
   - Only offer auto-update when the manager/channel combination supports it.
   - Map auto-update actions to installer-native commands.
   - Reuse the same provenance source for update prompts and execution.

## Migration Strategy

- Existing installs without provenance continue using heuristic detection.
- New installs write provenance at install time.
- After installer coverage is in place, auto-update can require provenance for managed flows.

## Open Questions

- Exact location of `install.json` on each platform.
- Whether Homebrew nightly should be recorded as `manager=brew` + `channel=nightly` or with a distinct package token only.
- Whether Go-installed/dev builds should remain unsupported for auto-update.

Reviewed all 15 commits (556-line new installer, README, `install.sh` error path, CI). Overall this is careful work — the PS 5.1 hazards are individually well-reasoned and the comments explain *why* rather than *what*. Findings, worst first:

## 1. `scoop prefix` output is parsed from a stream that deliberately carries stderr

`scripts/install.ps1:387`

```powershell
$scoopPrefix = ($prefixResult.Output | Select-Object -First 1).ToString().Trim()
```

`Invoke-Scoop` merges stderr into `Output` with `2>&1` — that merge is the whole point of the `$ErrorActionPreference` dance at line 72-76, whose own comment says scoop emits "update notices, deprecation warnings" on stderr. So `Select-Object -First 1` takes whatever scoop emitted first, which may be an `ErrorRecord` whose `.ToString()` is a warning message, not a path. The three `Split-Path -Parent` calls then produce a garbage `$scoopShim`, `Test-SamePath` fails, and the function throws *"Scoop installed Entire CLI, but its shim does not take priority on PATH"* after a completely successful install — with a manual-fix message pointing at a nonexistent directory.

You already have the shim location for free: `$scoopCommand.Source` (line 379) is `<root>\shims\scoop.exe`. Deriving `$scoopShim` from its parent removes both the parse and the triple `Split-Path`.

## 2. The PATH-conflict check can't see the case it exists to catch

`scripts/install.ps1:341-360, 499-526`

`Add-ToUserPath` prepends to the **User** PATH, but Windows composes the process PATH as machine-then-user. So a conflicting `entire.exe` in a machine PATH directory (a Program Files or Chocolatey install) always wins in a new terminal, no matter where it sits in the user PATH.

The verification at line 499 runs `Get-Command` against `$env:Path`, which the script just mutated in-process at line 355-357. So `$firstIsOurs` is true, the user is told *"The installed version takes priority"*, and their next terminal resolves the old binary. The in-session prepend is right for usability (and the caching comment is correct), but the *check* should be made against the PATH a new shell will see — machine PATH + the new user PATH — not against the mutated process PATH.

Related self-inflicted case: because this script prepends its own dir to the user PATH, a user who runs `install.ps1` without Scoop, later installs Scoop, and reruns hits the hard `throw` at line 407 telling them to fix PATH by hand.

## 3. `$LASTEXITCODE` read under `Set-StrictMode -Version 2.0`

`scripts/install.ps1:80`

`$LASTEXITCODE` does not exist until a native command runs in the session, and StrictMode 2.0 makes reading an unset variable terminating. The first thing `Install-Entire` does on a Scoop machine is `Invoke-Scoop bucket list`. In a shim directory PowerShell resolves `scoop.ps1` ahead of `scoop.cmd`, and an `ExternalScript` sets `$LASTEXITCODE` only if it calls `exit`. I could not verify scoop's current shim on this machine, so treat this as a risk rather than a confirmed break — but `$LASTEXITCODE = 0` immediately before the call costs one line and removes the question. (Line 486 is fine; that's a real `.exe`.)

## 4. `-InstallDir` is silently ignored when Scoop is present

`scripts/install.ps1:380-421` returns before `$resolvedInstallDir` is ever computed. `install.ps1 -InstallDir C:\tools` on a Scoop machine installs somewhere else and says nothing. Either warn, or let an explicit `-InstallDir` opt out of the Scoop path. Note the child-scope wrapper means `$PSBoundParameters` is unavailable inside, so distinguishing "explicit" from "default" needs the flag passed in at line 556.

## 5. CI covers argument parsing and nothing else

`.github/workflows/ci.yml:79-93` runs only `-Help` on both shells. That catches parse errors — worth having — but zero percent of the logic: architecture detection, the registry read, download, checksum matching, `Get-NormalizedPath`, the conflict check. Eleven of the fifteen commits on this branch are follow-up fixes to PS 5.1 breakage found by hand, which is exactly what a real run would have caught.

`windows-latest` has no Scoop, so a real install exercises the risky archive path directly:

```yaml
- name: Windows PowerShell 5 installer end-to-end
  shell: powershell
  run: .\scripts\install.ps1 -InstallDir "$env:RUNNER_TEMP\entire" -NoPathUpdate
```

Two steps, one per shell, and finding #3 above would either be confirmed or dismissed by the first run.

## 6. Ship-order dependency

`scripts/install.sh:64` now tells every Windows user to run `irm https://entire.io/install.ps1 | iex`, and the README makes it the primary Windows instruction. Nothing in this repo publishes that path — is the `entire.io/install.ps1` redirect already live? If not, this branch turns the existing Windows error message into a 404.

## Minor

- `scripts/install.ps1:143` — `default { throw "Unsupported architecture: $architecture" }` will fire on `x86` (32-bit PowerShell reading a 32-bit machine key). Fine, but the message doesn't say 32-bit Windows is unsupported, which is the actual situation.
- `install.sh` runs `entire curl-bash-post-install` (`install.sh:340`); `install.ps1` doesn't. Currently harmless — that command only wires zsh/bash/fish completion — but if PowerShell profile completion ever lands, this is the parity gap to remember. A comment saying the omission is deliberate would help.
- `Test-PathContains`/`-split ";"` doesn't handle quoted PATH entries. Rare enough to ignore; noting it so it isn't rediscovered.

Nothing here is a security problem — checksum verification, TLS 1.2 pinning, `LiteralPath` throughout, and the regex-anchored version validation all look right, and the `-UseBasicParsing` and `RuntimeInformation` comments are the kind that save the next reader an hour.

Two options. I recommend the first.

## A. Stop parsing `scoop prefix` — derive the shims dir from scoop itself (recommended)

The block's job isn't to locate where Scoop put `entire`; it's to check whether the **shim** wins on PATH. The shims directory is a property of the Scoop installation, and you already have it in hand at line 382: `Get-Command "scoop"` resolves to `…\scoop\shims\scoop.ps1` (or `.cmd`), whose parent *is* the shims dir. Since the install at line 121 is non-global, `entire.exe`'s shim lands in that same directory.

```powershell
        # Restrict to a real executable/script: Invoke-Scoop's exit-code
        # contract only holds for one, and .Source must be a path below.
        $scoopCommand = Get-Command "scoop" -CommandType Application, ExternalScript -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
        if ($SelectedChannel -eq "stable" -and $null -ne $scoopCommand) {
            # ... existing -InstallDir/-NoPathUpdate comment ...
            Install-EntireWithScoop

            # Verification only; the output is not parsed. Scoop's stderr is
            # merged into Output by design, so line 1 is not reliably a path.
            $prefixResult = Invoke-Scoop prefix entire
            if ($prefixResult.ExitCode -ne 0) {
                throw "Scoop installed Entire CLI, but its installation path could not be resolved."
            }

            # scoop lives in the shims directory it puts on PATH, and a
            # non-global `scoop install` shims entire.exe alongside it.
            $scoopShim = Join-Path (Split-Path -Parent $scoopCommand.Source) "entire.exe"
```

That deletes lines 393–395 — the fragile `Select-Object -First 1 … .ToString()` and the triple `Split-Path -Parent` — and keeps the `prefix` call as the post-install verification it effectively already is. Everything downstream (399, 403, 411, 416) is unchanged.

Two things to be aware of: `-CommandType Application, ExternalScript` means a shell *function* or alias named `scoop` no longer takes the Scoop branch and falls through to the archive install. I think that's the more correct behaviour — `Invoke-Scoop` reads `$LASTEXITCODE` right after the call, which a function needn't set (that's finding #3) — but it is a behaviour change, not just a refactor. Your install worked — `entire` 0.10.3 is in via Scoop. That line is cosmetic noise from a probe that's *expected* to fail.

**What produced it.** Line 110 runs `scoop prefix entire` purely to decide install-vs-update:

```powershell
$probe = Invoke-Scoop prefix entire
$isInstalled = $probe.ExitCode -eq 0
```

On a first install `entire` isn't there yet, so `scoop-prefix.ps1` hits its `abort "Could not find app path for '$app'."` and exits non-zero. The installer reads that correctly — hence `==> Installing Entire CLI with Scoop...` on the very next line, the install branch rather than the update branch.

**Why it isn't swallowed.** `Invoke-Scoop` captures with `2>&1`, which redirects only the error stream. But scoop's `abort` is `Write-Host $msg -f red` (as are `error`, `warn`, `info`, `success`), and since PowerShell 5.0 `Write-Host` writes to the *information* stream. `2>&1` neither captures nor suppresses that, so the message goes straight to your console, orphaned from the installer's own `==>` framing. It also never lands in `$probe.Output`, which is why the code can't detect and hide it.

That's the same mechanism that killed my finding #1 earlier — scoop's messages bypass the capture entirely — showing up here as the opposite symptom: not a corrupted parse, just a leak to the terminal.

You won't see it again on this machine; a rerun takes the update branch.

**If you want it gone.** The probe only needs the exit code, so discard every stream — matching the `*> $null` idiom already used for the post-install version check:

```powershell
    function Test-ScoopAppInstalled {
        param([string] $AppName)

        # scoop's abort/warn/info use Write-Host, i.e. the information stream,
        # which 2>&1 neither captures nor suppresses. A failed probe would
        # otherwise print "Could not find app path for '<app>'" to the console,
        # which reads as a failure during a successful first install.
        $previous = $ErrorActionPreference
        $ErrorActionPreference = "Continue"
        try {
            & "scoop" prefix $AppName *> $null
            return $LASTEXITCODE -eq 0
        }
        finally {
            $ErrorActionPreference = $previous
        }
    }
```

then `$isInstalled = Test-ScoopAppInstalled -AppName "entire"` at line 110-111. Deliberately not a blanket `*>&1` inside `Invoke-Scoop` — that would also swallow the `Extracting… done.` / `was installed successfully!` progress you got above, which is worth keeping.

content.text:
Yes — and pinning it down turned up something bigger, which your own transcript proves. Two parts.

## The narrow #3 scenario

The generated Scoop shim (`lib/core.ps1`, `shim` function) ends with:

```powershell
"if (`$MyInvocation.ExpectingInput) { `$input | & `$path $arg @args } else { & `$path $arg @args }",
"exit `$LASTEXITCODE"
```

So `$LASTEXITCODE` is read *inside the shim*, before our line 83 ever gets to it. And `scoop-prefix.ps1` on its **success** path just does `Write-Output $app_path` and falls off the end — no `exit`, no native command. So the sequence is:

1. Brand-new PowerShell session, no native command run yet, so `$LASTEXITCODE` doesn't exist.
2. `entire` is *already* installed via Scoop — i.e. an existing user re-running the installer to upgrade.
3. `scoop prefix entire` succeeds, sets nothing.
4. The shim's own `exit $LASTEXITCODE` reads an unset variable under strict mode → terminating error inside Scoop's shim.

The catch, and why I keep hedging: `scoop bucket list` runs first (line 95), and modern Scoop shells out to `git log -1` per bucket for the "Updated" column, which sets `$LASTEXITCODE` globally for the rest of the session. So step 4 is protected by accident, unless the machine has no buckets at all. That's narrow enough that I'd not have raised it on its own.

## What your transcript actually shows

`Could not find app path for 'entire'.` **printed to your console instead of being captured.**

`$output = & "scoop" @ScoopArgs 2>&1` captures the child's stdout. Had Scoop run as a separate process, its `Write-Host` would have landed in that redirected stdout and gone into `$output` — which the probe discards, so you'd never have seen it. You saw it. So `scoop` resolved to `scoop.ps1` and ran **in-process**, where `Write-Host` goes to the information stream and escapes both the `2>&1` and the assignment.

That matters because `Set-StrictMode` is *dynamically* scoped — it applies to the scope that sets it and every child scope. Line 28 sets `-Version 2.0` for the whole installer, so every line of Scoop we invoke runs under StrictMode 2.0: the shim, `scoop-install.ps1`, and everything they dot-source. Scoop isn't written for it. Under 2.0, referencing an unset variable, reading a non-existent property, or calling a function with method syntax all become terminating errors — anywhere in that codebase.

Your run got through `bucket list`, `prefix`, and a full `install`, so Scoop tolerated it on that path. That's the code we happened to execute on one machine and version, not a property we're entitled to rely on across Scoop releases.

## Fix

One line, same shape as the `$ErrorActionPreference` dance already in `Invoke-Scoop`, and it covers both parts — the shim's `exit $LASTEXITCODE` and all of Scoop's code:

```powershell
        $previous = $ErrorActionPreference
        $ErrorActionPreference = "Continue"
        Set-StrictMode -Off          # scoop runs in-process; 2.0 would leak into it
        try {
            $output = & "scoop" @ScoopArgs 2>&1
```

`Set-StrictMode -Off` inside `Invoke-Scoop` covers that function and its children only — the caller's scope keeps 2.0 on return, so our own code stays strict. It needs no `finally` restore for that reason, though matching the existing style wouldn't hurt.

Note the tradeoff: with strict mode off, an unset `$LASTEXITCODE` at line 83 yields `$null`, and `[int] $null` is `0` — a silent "success" rather than a throw. Since the shim always `exit`s, that shouldn't be reachable; if you want it airtight, `$LASTEXITCODE = 0` before the call makes the default explicit.

content.text:
The check answers "does `entire` resolve to us *right now*" — but line 378 just force-prepended our directory to `$env:Path`, so the answer is yes by construction. The question users actually care about, "will it resolve to us in a new terminal", is never asked. Since our write only ever lands in the **user** half of the PATH and Windows composes a new session's PATH as machine-then-user, any `entire.exe` sitting in a machine PATH directory outranks us there permanently, and today we print *"The installed version takes priority"* anyway.

## Proposal: derive the verdict from the PATH a new terminal will build

Two helpers next to the existing PATH functions:

```powershell
    function Get-FutureSessionPath {
        # What a new terminal will compose: machine first, then user. Our
        # prepend only ever lands in the user half, so it cannot outrank a
        # machine entry no matter where it sits within the user PATH.
        $parts = @(
            [Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable("Path", "Machine")
            [Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable("Path", "User")
        ) | Where-Object { -not [string]::IsNullOrWhiteSpace($_) }
        return ($parts -join ";")
    }

    function Get-FirstEntireInPath {
        param([AllowNull()] [string] $PathValue)

        # Only entire.exe: that is what both the archive install and the Scoop
        # shim produce. A hand-rolled entire.cmd wrapper is not considered.
        foreach ($entry in ($PathValue -split ";")) {
            $trimmed = $entry.Trim()
            if ([string]::IsNullOrWhiteSpace($trimmed)) { continue }
            try { $directory = Get-NormalizedPath -Path $trimmed } catch { continue }
            $candidate = Join-Path $directory "entire.exe"
            if (Test-Path -LiteralPath $candidate -PathType Leaf) { return $candidate }
        }
        return $null
    }
```

Then at the direct-install check (line 525-529), the precedence verdict comes from the future PATH while the *listing* of other installations keeps coming from `Get-Command`, which is what it's good at:

```powershell
            $pathCommands = Get-EntireOnPath
            $conflicting = @($pathCommands | Where-Object { -not (Test-SamePath -Left $_.Source -Right $installPath) })
            if ($conflicting.Count -gt 0) {
                $futureFirst = Get-FirstEntireInPath -PathValue (Get-FutureSessionPath)
                $firstIsOurs = Test-SamePath -Left $futureFirst -Right $installPath
```

`Test-SamePath` already returns `$false` for a null/blank left side, so a null `$futureFirst` needs no extra guard.

The message wants splitting to match, since the two situations have different remedies — in-session shadowing the user can fix by reordering their user PATH, versus a machine-PATH entry they must remove or elevate to outrank:

```powershell
                if (-not $firstIsOurs) {
                    Write-Host "! In a new terminal, 'entire' will resolve to: $futureFirst"
                    Write-Host "! Remove that installation, or move $resolvedInstallDir ahead of it."
                    Write-Host "! A machine-wide PATH entry always outranks your user PATH, so a"
                    Write-Host "! machine-level install must be removed rather than reordered."
```

## Same defect in the Scoop branch

Line 417 does the identical thing against `Get-EntireOnPath`, and Scoop's shims directory is likewise on the *user* PATH — so a machine-PATH `entire.exe` outranks the shim in a new terminal while the current session says otherwise, and that branch **throws** on a wrong verdict rather than warning. Both call sites should take the verdict from `Get-FirstEntireInPath` against the future PATH; that's the reason to factor the helpers rather than inline the logic at one site.

## What I'd leave alone

The in-process prepend at line 378 stays — making `entire` work immediately in the caller's shell is the right behaviour, and the comment about `Get-Command` caching is correct. This changes only which PATH the *verdict* is computed from.

Worth flagging honestly: I can't test any of this from here, and it touches the branch that currently hard-`throw`s. If you take it, it wants a real run on a machine with a planted `entire.exe` in a machine PATH directory — which is also the one case the current code gets wrong, so it's the test that matters.
